_comment: Aelgard Boneyard Wastes bestiary. Desert of bone-sand and mummy-kings; the sand is literally ground fossil, and old dynasties still hold legal title to plots of dune. Tone: dry, formal, legally-encumbered dread.
_region_tone: heat-shimmer, bone-dust wind, mummy bureaucracy. Undead here are not wild; they are civil servants.

monsters.name: Bone scarab
monsters.examine: A beetle the size of a breadloaf. Bites.
bible: Boneyard scarabs nest inside the ribcages of the larger dead. Every major tomb has a scarab population; every minor one used to, before the last century's dig-overs.

They groom the bones they nest in, which archivists consider a religious service and tomb-robbers consider a hindrance. Scarab-grooming has kept certain royal skeletons articulate enough to still swear legal oaths.
Killing a scarab is not a crime, but removing one from a sealed tomb triggers a Crypt Assembly inspection within the week.
monsters.habitat: ribcages of the large dead, cracked sarcophagi, the Second Plot dunes
monsters.anti_pattern_note: scarab-in-sarcophagus encounters are a 3-wave spawn; killing the queen scarab stops the waves.

monsters.name: Salt stalker
monsters.examine: A desert cat with brine in its veins.
bible: Salt stalkers are the Boneyard's apex predator in the shade-hours — dusk to dawn. They are the size of a wolf, the colour of bone-sand, and they spray a saline mist from glands under the tongue.

Their hide is treasured; stitched together it makes sun-resistant travel armour. This creates a grey market in salt-stalker hides which the Boneyard rangers cannot legally shut down because the stalkers are technically not protected.
A mature salt stalker will trail a caravan for three nights before attacking on the fourth. Caravans that know the rhythm drop a sacrificial donkey on the third night.
monsters.habitat: Boneyard dunes in shade-hours, caravan routes, oasis peripheries
monsters.reagent_callout: Salt-stalker hide (1/12) crafts into sun-cloak (heat-resistance layer for Glass Desert deep travel).

monsters.name: Dust dweller
bible: Dust dwellers are the middle-sized predator in the Boneyard food chain. Lizardlike, sand-tongued, bone-ridged; they burrow under the loose dune-top and wait for footfall.
A caravan guide can spot their burrow-mounds; most travellers cannot, which is why dust dweller attacks are a leading cause of caravan fatality in the Boneyard ledger.
Killed, their flat fangs are harvested as striking tools — they are harder than steel, lighter than stone, and they take a glass-edge well.
monsters.habitat: open dune-tops, just below sand-surface, away from oases
monsters.reagent_callout: Dust-dweller tooth (1/6) crafts into glass-edge chisel for Glass Desert crystal-cutting.

monsters.name: Mummy guardian
monsters.examine: Wrapped linen and a grudge against trespass.
bible: Mummy guardians were, in life, appointed civil servants of their dynasty — city wardens, treasury clerks, chief-of-funerals. Their afterlife contract includes guarding the tomb where they are interred. The contract is renewed every century by the Crypt Assembly; most guardians have been on duty three hundred years or more.
They do not hunt. They patrol. Their patrol route is exactly the same today as the day they were wrapped. You can time a crossing by their gait.
They are not mindless. A guardian can be negotiated with if you carry a valid tomb-writ from the Crypt Assembly. The writs are expensive and the Assembly is not generous.
monsters.habitat: tomb-corridors, sand-buried burial complexes, the Avenue of Names
monsters.anti_pattern_note: tomb-writ item bypasses aggro. A player with the writ should never be attacked by a guardian. Designers, check your encounter gates.

monsters.name: Pharaoh lich
monsters.examine: He ran a kingdom. He hasn't stopped.
bible: A Pharaoh lich is what remains when the Crypt Assembly fails to relocate a Pharaoh on the centenary of his interment. Missed a paperwork deadline; the tomb seal lapses; the Pharaoh rises and resumes, as far as his memory permits, the duties of office.

He issues decrees. He collects tolls (by force, from passing travellers). He holds court (in a tomb chamber, for an audience of mummies). A particularly persistent lich will have accumulated a staff of reanimated clerks.

Killing a Pharaoh lich is a minor diplomatic crisis. The Assembly will deny responsibility, the dynasty's descendants will demand reparations, and the Sootworks ambassador will issue a strongly-worded note. Expect follow-up quests.
monsters.habitat: failed-upkeep tombs, the Court of Sand, old-dynasty sarcophagus vaults
monsters.reagent_callout: Pharaoh's seal (unique drop 1/192) — reagent for Sand-crown diadem (magic-boost + slayer-niche vs mummy-tag).

monsters.name: Sand wyvern
monsters.examine: Dragon-kin that learned to swim through dune.
bible: Sand wyverns are cousins of the dragons who adapted to the Boneyard conditions. They can swim through loose sand as easily as a pike through water, and surface only to strike or to lay eggs.

They hunt by seismic sense — detecting footfall at distance. Caravans crossing wyvern-territory use low-impact camel-skeel shoes that dampen the step-signal. The shoes are prohibitively expensive outside the Boneyard.
Their hide is thermal-insulating; harvested and cured, it forms the inner liner of the best Glass Desert survival suits.
monsters.habitat: deep-dune territory beyond the Third Plot, the Wyvern Pass
monsters.reagent_callout: Wyvern-scale liner (1/32) — reagent for the Glass Desert endgame survival suit (heat resistance + magic defence).

monsters.name: Bone servant
monsters.examine: A servant who didn't get the memo.
bible: When a Boneyard noble dies, the customary funeral includes the ritual of 'released service' — formally freeing the servants who are interred alongside. Occasionally a servant is not released because the ritual-master forgot; occasionally the servant stays anyway, out of loyalty or out of habit.
A bone servant still performs his duties, in ghostly simulacrum. Some carry trays. Some sweep. Some bow to travellers and offer absent refreshments.
They attack only if their master's tomb is desecrated. This is the only reason to fight them, and it is not a good one.
monsters.habitat: noble-plot tombs, old servant-quarters, ritually-incomplete burials
monsters.anti_pattern_note: NEVER attack an unprovoked servant. Combat triggers a tomb-desecration status effect (negative diary impact).

monsters.name: Glass crawler
monsters.examine: A many-legged thing of fused sand. It is also a mirror.
bible: Glass crawlers form at the border between the Boneyard and Glass Desert. Intense heat fuses bone-sand into crystalline exoskeleton; the creature inside is mostly instinct. The exoskeleton reflects — so the crawler sees you as you see it.
Looking directly into the thorax reveals a distorted version of the viewer. This has been used, in several famous Boneyard paintings, to depict the soul-condition of the painter.
Killed, the shell fractures into usable crystal shards — valuable for glass-smithing if taken fresh, before the shards re-fuse.
monsters.habitat: the Boneyard-Glass Desert border, the Fused Flats
monsters.reagent_callout: Fresh crystal shard (0/5, 30-min timer decay) — reagent for glass-sharp blade variants.

monsters.name: Tomb robber
monsters.examine: The living kind. Armed and nervous.
bible: Tomb robbers are professionals. They work in pairs, carry glass-lanterns, and have maps. They are specifically NOT mercenaries or bandits; those make too much noise and get killed by the dead residents.
A tomb robber will flee from a patrol, fight a tomb-raiding competitor to the death, and bargain with a paying customer. The player falls into the latter category if approached correctly.
The Crypt Assembly pays a bounty of 500 coin per robber turned in alive. Most robbers know this. Most robbers therefore do not surrender.
monsters.habitat: active tomb-complexes, specifically the Second Plot sector
monsters.anti_pattern_note: bargaining branch (hand over 100gp) triggers a short trade interaction. Not every mob is a fight.

monsters.name: Mirage warrior
monsters.examine: Not quite there. Not quite not.
bible: Mirage warriors are desert-optical illusions that have forgotten they were illusions. Over decades of appearing to desperate travellers, a particular mirage can accrete enough belief to solidify just enough to throw a spear.
They are fickle. A mirage warrior may become solid only when in direct sunlight and only at certain distances. The math is elaborate. Boneyard rangers teach it in the Dune-Craft training.
Killed, they dissolve into a cloud of irrelevant memories — travellers frequently report knowing, briefly, the name of an uncle they never had.
monsters.habitat: open Boneyard dunes, specifically the Long Mirage south of the Second Plot
monsters.anti_pattern_note: visible-only-at-certain-distance is a real mechanic. Do not render the mob at melee range.

monsters.name: Vulture swarm
bible: A Boneyard vulture swarm is five or more of the carrion-birds acting in coordinated flocking. They are not a hive organism; they are individually smart, collectively stupid, and aggregately lethal.

They descend on the dying and on the foolish. Travellers who sit down to rest at the wrong time of day are swarmed. The correct counter is a lit torch plus a steady step forward; the swarm scatters, regroups, and leaves.
Boneyard caravans set torches at sundown for this reason. Not for visibility.
monsters.habitat: any open sand, concentrated along caravan routes at dusk
monsters.anti_pattern_note: torch item (common regional) reduces aggro. Encounter design should assume the player may be mid-cast and torch-less.

monsters.name: Oasis grindworm
bible: Grindworms are the Boneyard's reason oases do not expand. The worm bores through the water-table from below and drains the aquifer over three to five years per oasis. Most oases have a grindworm cycle.
They surface only at dusk to mate. This is a 30-minute window weekly. Dune-hunters time grindworm contracts to this window.
The worm's grinding-plate is high-carbon; refined, it makes an exceptional heavy cleaver.
monsters.habitat: active oases, the aquifer below, the Palm Retreat specifically
monsters.reagent_callout: Grindworm plate (1/32) — reagent for the Boneyard endgame heavy cleaver 'Aquifer's End'.

monsters.name: Nomad warrior
bible: Boneyard nomad tribes are not Crown-affiliated. They are older than any Crown and they know it. A nomad warrior will approach any traveller within tribal territory to demand papers.
'Papers' means any token showing allegiance, a trade-letter, or a ceremonial gift. A jewel works. So does a good joke delivered in the tribal dialect.

A warrior who receives no papers and no joke will first attempt to detain, not to kill. Resisting detention upgrades the encounter to combat. Killing a nomad warrior triggers tribal blood-debt the player carries for the rest of the account.
monsters.habitat: nomad tribal territory — the First Plot and the Northern Dunes
monsters.anti_pattern_note: DO NOT flag-kill. Killed-without-provocation nomads carry durable blood-debt. Only hostile-aggressed kills are safe.

monsters.name: Sand genie
monsters.examine: A being of compressed desert. Will bargain. Will cheat.
bible: Sand genies are one of the two surviving true-magical native species in the Boneyard (the other is the scarab queen, arguably). A genie binds itself to an object — usually a lamp, but also rings, daggers, or, in one famous case, a well-rope — and grants wishes to whoever holds it.
They cheat on every wish. This is common knowledge. People wish anyway. The cheats are not malicious; they are aesthetic.
A freed genie is dangerous until re-bound. Combat is their restraint protocol.
monsters.habitat: ancient-bound objects, lamp-caves, the Well of the Third Plot
monsters.reagent_callout: Genie-lamp fragment (1/128) — reagent for the Three-Wish Lamp (skilling-boost consumable, limited charges).

region_flavor_drops: Wyvern-scale liner (1/32 — reagent: Glass Desert survival suit)
Grindworm plate (1/32 — reagent: Aquifer's End heavy cleaver)
